title: Social teaching at home
hookLine: how we shop, work, vote and spend time, weighed in conscience

lines: A RECEIPT, A CALENDAR, A BALLOT.
cards: A receipt from the grocery store. A calendar with this week's hours on it. A ballot, or a reminder that one is coming.
A phone with a screen-time report you'd rather not open. Not one of them looks like a papal letter.
But this block of the path has walked through letters on wages, peace, migrants and the earth, and every one ends up here, in small choices on an ordinary day.
Today the big teaching comes home, and meets a word the Church takes very seriously: conscience.

teach.b: You met conscience on day three hundred ten; here it goes to work. The Second Vatican Council calls it a person's most secret core and sanctuary, where they are alone with God, whose voice echoes in their depths.
The Catechism adds that a conscience needs forming, by prayer, scripture, the Church's teaching and honest advice. It isn't just a feeling. It's where choices get weighed.

Pope Benedict the Sixteenth wrote that buying something is always a moral act, not only an economic one. A price tag hides a chain of hands: who grew it, who sewed it, who hauled it, what it did to the land.
Conscience at the checkout means letting that chain be seen, at least sometimes. Then work and voting.

teach.h: PRINCIPLES ON THE BALLOT, NOT A PARTY.
teach.b: Earlier this block taught that work has dignity, and that the Church offers principles, not a party platform. So Catholics can weigh the same teaching and still vote differently.
The Church asks that the weighing be honest, with every principle on the scale, not just the convenient ones. Then time.
A Sabbath, rest, a meal with the family, an hour for someone lonely: how time is spent says what matters.

teach.h: FAITHFUL IN THAT WHICH IS LEAST.
teach.b: Jesus gives the small-and-great rule in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "He that is faithful in that which is least, is faithful also in that which is greater." Social teaching is rarely lived at a summit.
It's lived at a register, an inbox, a ballot box, a kitchen table, one ordinary choice at a time.

how: Catholics form their consciences through prayer, scripture and Church teaching, and some use an examination of conscience that includes how they spend, work, vote and treat others; parishes and bishops' conferences publish guides for this.

games.q: what does “social teaching at home” mean?
o: a Catholic rule to buy only from Catholic shops
a family's own set of house rules for chores
the Church's big principles lived in small choices

games.q: social teaching at home — tap the pairs.
p: always a moral act, said Benedict XVI

s: in Church teaching, conscience is simply a gut feeling
the Catechism says a conscience needs forming, by prayer, scripture, teaching and advice.
Benedict XVI wrote that buying is a moral act, not only an economic one
a price tag hides a chain of hands.
social teaching tells Catholics which party to vote for
it offers principles; Catholics weigh them and may vote differently.

games.q: you're at the checkout with two nearly identical shirts. one is cheaper, and nobody knows who made it. what does conscience at the checkout ask?
o: pause and let the chain of hands be seen.
it's only shopping; conscience isn't involved.
games.why: Benedict XVI wrote that buying is always a moral act. the ask is to look, and to weigh, not to stop living.

practice: Choose just one habit, something you buy every week, how a typical evening goes, how you talk about people you disagree with, and turn it gently in your hand like an object.
Who does it touch, who made it possible, does it line up with what you care about? No verdict yet; if you pray, bring the habit to God and ask for light.

wordCard.voice: Social teaching at home. The Church's big principles, weighed in conscience in small choices: what you buy, how you work and vote, how you spend your time.

orig.note: Latin: conscience, the word the Church's Latin documents use for it.

carryVoice: Your line: conscience at the checkout. Every price tag hides a chain of hands. One more day on the path.
